content.title: About
content.content: Beaver meat is obtained from wild or farm‑raised beavers. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor with nutty notes and a firm yet tender texture. Beaver is used in traditional northern dishes and modern cuisine as steaks, stews, and ground meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beaver meat is high in protein and relatively low in fat compared with other wild meats.
Beavers are famous for building dams, and their fur and teeth have been utilized by humans for centuries.
In some cultures, beaver is considered a delicacy and is served on special occasions.
Beavers undergo a long winter dormancy, so their meat is typically harvested in the autumn when they have built up fat reserves.
Beaver meat is often compared to rabbit meat because of its similar tenderness and flavor profile.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beaver provides a high amount of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other wild meats, beaver contains moderate fat levels, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Beaver is a good source of iron, zinc, and phosphorus, contributing to healthy blood and bones.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Wild beavers obtain omega‑3s from their plant diet, resulting in modest amounts of these beneficial fats in the meat.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Like any wild meat, beaver can harbor parasites; thorough cooking is essential.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergies to wild game, including beaver.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Beaver contains purines, so people with gout should limit consumption.

items.title: Environmental contaminants
items.content: Beavers can accumulate heavy metals from polluted waterways; obtain meat from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beaver can be pan‑seared, braised, roasted, or grilled. For extra tenderness, marinate the meat in olive oil, garlic, and herbs for 2‑4 hours. Cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F) to ensure safety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store beaver in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer keeping, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 6 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage are present.

content.title: About
content.content: The Cookie Fig Bar (2691) is a soft baked snack bar made with whole dried figs, rolled oats, honey, and a touch of butter. It offers a sweet, slightly caramelized flavor with a distinct fruity aroma of fig and a pleasantly crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Figs are one of the oldest cultivated fruits, grown for over 6,000 years in the Mediterranean and the Middle East.
Dried figs retain up to 80 % of their original nutritional value, including fiber and minerals.
Cookie bars are made without artificial colors or flavorings.
Each bar provides about 12 g of natural sugars derived from honey and figs.
The product is packaged in a biodegradable wrapper suitable for composting.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Figs and oats supply a substantial amount of dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Natural antioxidants
items.content: The fig bar contains polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from honey and figs provide a quick and sustained energy release.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in figs promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Honey or butter allergy
items.content: The product contains honey and a small amount of butter, which may trigger reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The bar contains natural sugars; people with diabetes should account for it in their daily intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One bar (~45 g) provides about 200 kcal, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The Cookie Fig Bar is convenient as an on‑the‑go snack, can be added to yogurt or muesli, or used as a sweet accent in dessert recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bars in a cool, dry place in their sealed packaging. For longer storage (over 3 months) keep them refrigerated to preserve the crunchy texture.

kidney-beans-from-dried-no-added-fat.title: Kidney beans, from dried, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are dried red beans that contain no added fat. After drying they retain high levels of protein, fiber, and complex carbohydrates. The beans are typically boiled before eating, making them a versatile ingredient for soups, stews, salads, and vegetarian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name "kidney bean" comes from its reddish‑brown color and kidney‑like shape.
The beans are rich in antioxidants, especially flavonoids that give them their vivid hue.
Dried beans can be stored for up to a year in a cool, dry place.
Kidney beans are a staple in Latin American, Mediterranean, and Asian cuisines.
Soaking dried beans for 4–12 hours before cooking reduces cooking time and improves digestibility.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of dry beans provides about 24 g of protein, making it valuable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: Beans supply iron for oxygen transport and folate essential for DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Dried kidney beans contain virtually no fat, fitting well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in beans help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Toxic compounds in raw beans
items.content: Raw kidney beans contain phytohaemagglutinin, a toxic glycoside. It must be destroyed by boiling for at least 10 minutes.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to legumes.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause increased gas in sensitive people; proper soaking and cooking reduce this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak dried beans in water for 4–12 hours, drain, then boil for 60–90 minutes until tender. Cooked kidney beans are used in chili, soups, salads, veggie burgers, and as a side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored they keep quality for up to 12 months. Cooked beans can be refrigerated for 4‑5 days.

mayonnaise-reduced-fat-with-olive-oil.title: Reduced Fat Mayonnaise with Olive Oil

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced fat mayonnaise with olive oil is a lighter version of classic mayonnaise, where part of the vegetable oil is replaced by olive oil and the overall fat level is lowered using water and stabilizers. The product retains a creamy texture and characteristic taste while providing fewer calories and more beneficial monounsaturated fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Olive oil gives the mayonnaise a subtle fruity aroma.
Fat reduction is achieved with emulsifiers that keep water stably dispersed.
Often chosen by people watching their weight but not wanting to give up the familiar flavor.
Olive‑oil based mayonnaise tends to be more stable during storage than versions made with refined oils.
In many markets it is marketed as a "healthier" alternative for salads and sandwiches.

items.title: Lower Calorie Content
items.content: Reduced fat means fewer calories per serving compared with traditional mayonnaise.

items.title: Monounsaturated Fatty Acids
items.content: Olive oil is rich in oleic acid, which supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Vitamin E
items.content: Olive oil provides vitamin E, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Easier Digestion
items.content: Emulsifiers and added water make the product lighter on the stomach.

items.title: No Trans Fats
items.content: Unlike some conventional mayonnaises, this version contains no trans fats.

items.title: Egg Allergy
items.content: Traditional mayonnaise contains egg yolk, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sodium Content
items.content: Despite lower fat, the product may still contain a notable amount of salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Shelf Life After Opening
items.content: Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 1‑2 weeks.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some formulations include preservatives that may not be suitable for those avoiding additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use reduced fat olive oil mayonnaise as a salad dressing, sandwich spread, in rolls, or as a base for sauces. It works well in recipes that require a creamy texture while keeping calories lower.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the product in the refrigerator at 2 °C‑6 °C. After opening, seal tightly to prevent air exposure. Do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Octopus salad, Puerto Rican style is a traditional dish from Puerto Rico made with boiled octopus, fresh vegetables, lime juice, olive oil, and aromatic spices. It offers a bright, refreshing flavor with citrus notes and a mild heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is often served in hot weather as a light appetizer or side.
Octopus is considered a symbol of the sea and abundance in Puerto Rican cuisine.
The classic recipe includes green onion, cilantro, and finely chopped habanero pepper.
It is commonly accompanied by plantain tortillas or cassava crackers.
Authentic versions use lime juice rather than lemon for a distinctive aroma.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Octopus provides high‑quality marine protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Despite its rich taste, the salad is relatively low in calories, making it diet‑friendly.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Octopus contains iron, zinc, and selenium, supporting immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood, including octopus, is a good source of omega‑3s beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The salad supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, important for nervous system health and energy metabolism.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to octopus.

items.title: Heavy metal accumulation
items.content: Octopus can accumulate toxins; purchase only from reputable sources.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If using a prepared dressing, watch the salt level, especially for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as an appetizer or light meal. It pairs well with plantain tortillas, cassava crackers, or simply with a spoon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese Pizza, Gluten-Free Thick Crust is a flavorful pizza made on a gluten‑free dough with an extra‑thick crust, topped with melted cheese and aromatic herbs. The rice‑ and corn‑based dough gives a soft yet sturdy base, while the cheese adds a rich, creamy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free dough allows people with celiac disease to enjoy pizza safely.
A thick crust holds more sauce and cheese, making each bite juicier.
The cheese blend often combines mozzarella and cheddar for optimal melt.
Traditional gluten‑free dough uses a mix of rice, potato, and tapioca flours.
This pizza style pairs well with additional toppings like vegetables, ham, or mushrooms.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Cheese and optional protein toppings (e.g., chicken) provide high‑quality protein.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in gluten
items.content: The gluten‑free crust is suitable for those with gluten intolerance.

items.title: May contain probiotics (when using fermented cheeses)
items.content: Certain cheeses can contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy proteins should avoid this pizza.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauce can be salty, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Thick crust and cheese make the dish energy‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may need lactose‑free cheese alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into portions. Add fresh vegetables, herbs, or a spicy sauce to taste. For a lighter option, use lactose‑free or vegan cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the crust crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach, frozen and cooked with added vegetable oil, is a quick‑defrost product that retains most of the nutrients of fresh spinach. It is convenient for making soups, sauces, casseroles and other dishes without washing or preparing fresh leaves.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen spinach is a staple ingredient in many ready‑to‑cook meals such as soups, sauces and baked dishes.
Rapid freezing preserves vitamins A, C and K as well as minerals like iron and magnesium.
A small amount of oil improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins, especially vitamin K.
Spinach belongs to the Amaranth family and has been cultivated since ancient Egyptian times.
Frozen spinach has a much longer shelf life than fresh spinach.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Good source of iron
items.content: Iron supports oxygen transport in the blood and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Spinach can help maintain a balanced energy intake during weight‑management diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oil
items.content: Some people may react to the oil used in the product.

items.title: Loss of some vitamins during long storage
items.content: Vitamin C can degrade over time in frozen storage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thawed spinach can be added to soups, sauces, omelets, pasta, casseroles and smoothies. It serves as a ready‑to‑use vegetable base without further preparation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen spinach in its original packaging in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.
